events.text: A volcanic ash bed within glacial deposits in northwestern Canada shows the Sturtian glaciation under way by 716.5 million years ago. The rocks then lay near the equator, so the ice reached the sea at low latitudes.
events.title: The Sturtian ice age

events.text: Today’s chart starts the Ediacaran 635 million years ago, at the end of the Cryogenian. In the snowball hypothesis, a global ice age ends abruptly once volcanoes raise carbon dioxide to about 350 times the modern level.
events.title: The Ediacaran begins

events.text: Soft-bodied organisms far larger and more complex than anything before appear about 575 million years ago. At Mistaken Point, Newfoundland, the oldest are dated to 574.17 ± 0.66 million years.
events.title: The first large, complex life

events.text: Today’s chart puts the base of the Cambrian at 538.8 ± 0.6 million years ago. Dated rocks in Namibia give 538.6–538.8. Scotese’s atlas, drawn on an older timescale, uses 542.
events.title: The Cambrian begins

events.text: In Namibia the last Ediacaran fossils and the first burrows of mobile animals are less than 410,000 years apart, ending 538.58 ± 0.19 million years ago. Through the early Cambrian many animal groups then appear as fossils, apparently within a few million years.
events.title: Burrowing animals take over

events.text: The earliest widely accepted spores of land plants come from rocks about 475 million years old. Plant fragments from Ordovician rocks of Oman show they grew in sporangia and point to relatives of liverworts.
events.title: The oldest spores of land plants

events.text: In the Hirnantian, the Ordovician’s last age, which begins 445.2 million years ago, a short, intense glaciation at the South Pole came with two pulses of extinction that removed about 85% of marine species.
events.title: End-Ordovician mass extinction

events.text: Larger fossils of land plants, not just their spores, appear in the Late Silurian, about 425 million years ago, some 50 million years after the oldest spores.
events.title: Plants big enough to see

events.text: Trees and forests arose in the Middle Devonian. Stumps at Gilboa, New York, belong to tree-fern-like plants at least 26 feet (8 m) tall; nearby Cairo, New York, has the oldest forest yet found.
events.title: The first forests

events.text: Sea life crashed at the boundary between the Frasnian and Famennian ages, 372.15 million years ago by today’s chart. In Raup and Sepkoski’s 1982 counts it stood out from the background but, unlike the other four, was not statistically significant.
events.title: Late Devonian mass extinction

events.text: Wetland forests of the tropics began in the Serpukhovian, which today’s chart starts 330.3 million years ago, as falling sea level exposed wide shelves. They spread dramatically late in the Bashkirian.
events.title: The coal forests begin

events.text: From the late Mississippian into the Permian, Gondwana collided with North America, raising the Appalachians and joining the continents into Pangaea. By today’s chart the late Mississippian begins 330.3 million years ago.
events.title: Pangaea comes together

events.text: Early in the Kasimovian, about 305 million years ago, the tropical coal forests collapsed and shrank by more than half. Among amphibians and reptiles, extinctions peaked and separate local faunas appeared for the first time.
events.title: The coal forests collapse

events.text: The most severe extinction of the last 542 million years happened between 251.941 and 251.880 million years ago. Estimates of marine species lost run from about 81% to more than 90%. Siberian lava eruptions are the leading suspect.
events.title: End-Permian mass extinction

events.text: About 230 million years ago, in rocks now in northwestern Argentina, the earliest dinosaurs were already the main hunters and small plant-eaters in that part of Pangaea.
events.title: Early dinosaurs

events.text: A partial skull from Crosby County, Texas, about 225 million years old, was described as the oldest mammal, at least 10 million years older than any found before. It is too incomplete to place exactly.
events.title: One of the oldest mammals

events.text: Major losses on land and in the sea. The first eruptions of the Central Atlantic lava province match the extinction in time; the lava came in four pulses over about 600,000 years.
events.title: End-Triassic mass extinction

events.text: Central Atlantic magma, now found across more than 2.7 million square miles (7 million km²) on both sides of the Atlantic, peaked about 200 million years ago as Pangaea began to break apart.
events.title: Pangaea begins to split

events.text: About 195 million years ago lived a mammal relative with an estimated weight of 2 grams (0.07 ounce). Its middle-ear bones were already separate from the jaw, as in living mammals.
events.title: A mammal relative weighing 2 grams

events.text: A 160-million-year-old fossil from China was described as the oldest known member of the group that includes all placental mammals, about 35 million years older than the previous record.
events.title: Oldest relative of placental mammals

events.text: Water plants from the Yixian Formation of Liaoning, China, at least 124.6 million years old, enclose their seeds in carpels, as flowering plants do, but have no petals or sepals.
events.title: Early flowering plants

events.text: An asteroid struck what is now Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula. Its debris forms a single layer found worldwide at the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, and dating puts the impact within 32,000 years of the extinction.
events.title: Asteroid impact at Chicxulub

events.text: One of the three largest extinctions of the last 500 million years ended the non-avian dinosaurs. A synthesis of the boundary rocks concludes the impact triggered it; the Deccan lava eruptions in India overlapped it, and how much they added is still debated.
events.title: End-Cretaceous mass extinction

events.text: Thousands of billions of metric tons of carbon entered the ocean and air in less than 20,000 years, and global temperature rose 9–14 °F (5–8 °C). The whole event lasted about 200,000 years.
events.title: Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum

events.text: Near the Eocene–Oligocene boundary, about 34 million years ago, permanent ice sheets first appeared on Antarctica, growing in two rapid steps.
events.title: Ice sheets form on Antarctica

events.text: A review of geological, fossil and genetic evidence puts the formation of the Isthmus of Panama around 2.8 million years ago, and finds the case for a much older isthmus inconclusive.
events.title: The Isthmus of Panama forms

events.text: Nearly all ice sheets stood at their largest from 26,500 years ago until 19,000–20,000 years ago, when stronger northern summer sunshine began the melt.
events.title: The Last Glacial Maximum

look_for.label: Glacial rocks, Yukon
look_for.text: Rocks now in northwestern Canada hold glacial deposits 716.5 million years old, laid down near the equator.

look_for.label: Mistaken Point fossils
look_for.text: Some of the oldest large, complex fossils, 574 million years old and younger, lie on rock surfaces here in Newfoundland.

look_for.label: Boundary rocks, Namibia
look_for.text: A section in Namibia dates the change from Ediacaran life to Cambrian burrowers to 538.99–538.58 million years ago.

look_for.label: Appalachians
look_for.text: Raised by collisions in the Ordovician, the Devonian and, as Pangaea assembled, from the late Mississippian into the Permian.

look_for.label: Earliest plant fragments
look_for.text: Spore-bearing fragments of early land plants, probably related to liverworts, come from Ordovician rocks now in Oman.

look_for.label: Gilboa fossil forest
look_for.text: Stumps of some of the earliest trees, tree-fern-like plants at least 26 feet (8 m) tall, stand in rock at Gilboa, New York.

look_for.label: Meishan, China
look_for.text: The reference section for the Permian–Triassic boundary; its ash beds date the extinction to an interval of 60,000 ± 48,000 years.

look_for.label: Siberian Traps
look_for.text: The leading suspect for the end-Permian extinction: lava erupted here before, during and after it, and magma intruded underground from its start.

look_for.label: Ischigualasto, Argentina
look_for.text: Rocks of the Ischigualasto Formation hold some of the earliest dinosaurs, about 230 million years old.

look_for.label: Oldest mammal, Texas
look_for.text: A skull about 225 million years old from Crosby County, Texas, described as the oldest mammal.

look_for.label: Atlantic magma, Brazil
look_for.text: Central Atlantic province magma extends over about 965,000 square miles (2.5 million km²) of north and central Brazil.

look_for.label: Yixian Formation, China
look_for.text: Water plants at least 124.6 million years old, among the earliest flowering plants, come from these rocks.

look_for.label: Chicxulub crater
look_for.text: The buried crater of the impact that ended the Cretaceous lies under the Yucatán Peninsula.

look_for.label: Deccan Traps
look_for.text: One study dates over 90% of these lavas to under a million years, about 75% after the extinction; another finds a surge began before it.

look_for.label: Himalaya
look_for.text: Watch India close on Asia. When their collision began is still argued.

look_for.label: East Antarctica
look_for.text: Permanent ice sheets first grew on Antarctica about 34 million years ago; Scotese’s maps paint East Antarctic ice earlier, from 44.6 million years ago.

look_for.label: Isthmus of Panama
look_for.text: Formed around 2.8 million years ago, joining North and South America.

note: Written for this app. Every number in a text is mapped in `numbers` to the source it comes from; ages named as ICS ages are from timescale.json, map ages from Scotese's Table 1. Pins are present-day positions, rotated with the PALEOMAP plate given.

periods.name: Quaternary
periods.text: Map 1 is today’s world, the reference for every other map. Map 2 is Scotese’s Last Glacial Maximum, 21,000 years ago, painted white over Canada and northern Europe. Nearly all ice sheets stood at their largest from 26,500 until 19,000–20,000 years ago; then stronger northern summer sunshine started the melt, and meltwater raised the sea. On the map: switch between the two and compare.

periods.name: Neogene
periods.text: The continents sit close to where they are today; the changes are at the edges. The Isthmus of Panama formed around 2.8 million years ago, joining North and South America. The review behind that date finds the evidence for a much older isthmus inconclusive. Antarctica is painted white on every Neogene map. On the map: follow the Himalaya pin as India keeps pushing north, and turn on today’s coasts to compare.

periods.name: Paleogene
periods.text: The Paleogene begins right after the asteroid impact that closed the Cretaceous. About 56 million years ago a vast release of carbon warmed the globe by 9–14 °F (5–8 °C): the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum. About 34 million years ago permanent ice sheets first formed on Antarctica. India closed on Asia; when their collision began is still argued. On the map: Scotese paints ice on East Antarctica from 44.6 million years ago, earlier than the permanent sheets the rocks date to about 34.

periods.name: Cretaceous
periods.text: Flowering plants appear: water plants from China at least 124.6 million years old already enclose their seeds in carpels. South America and Africa pull apart and the South Atlantic opens. Shallow seas spread over the continents; on the 80.3-million-year map one splits North America in two. The period ends with the Chicxulub impact and the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs. On the map: India is an island, heading north.

periods.name: Jurassic
periods.text: Pangaea breaks up. Central Atlantic magma, now found across more than 2.7 million square miles (7 million km²) of the Americas, Europe and Africa, peaked about 200 million years ago as the breakup began. Dinosaurs dominated the land for the next 136 million years. Some close relatives of mammals were tiny: one from about 195 million years ago weighed an estimated 2 grams. On the map: a narrow sea opens between North America and Africa.

periods.name: Triassic
periods.text: The Triassic begins just after the most severe extinction of the last 542 million years. Some of the earliest dinosaurs, about 230 million years old, come from northwestern Argentina, where they were already the main hunters and small plant-eaters. A 225-million-year-old skull from Texas was described as the oldest mammal. The period ends with another mass extinction, timed with the first eruptions of a huge lava province. On the map: Pangaea, whole, reaches the South Pole.

periods.name: Permian
periods.text: Pangaea is whole: one landmass curving around a great bay of ocean to the east. On these maps the great white sheet in the south shrinks to a small patch by 280 million years ago; the end of this ice age is the only switch from icehouse to greenhouse recorded since plants covered the land. The Permian ends in the most severe extinction known. Estimates of marine species lost run from about 81% to more than 90%. The Siberian Traps eruptions are the leading suspect; how they killed is debated.

periods.name: Carboniferous
periods.text: Coal forests, the wetland forests of the tropics, began in the Serpukhovian as falling sea level exposed wide shelves, spread late in the Bashkirian, and collapsed early in the Kasimovian, about 305 million years ago. Ice sheets came and went over southern Gondwana in the longest ice age of the last 539 million years. Gondwana’s collision with North America began building Pangaea. On the map: the far south is painted white from 332.5 million years ago.

periods.name: Devonian
periods.text: Forests appear. Trees and forests arose in the Middle Devonian, 393–383 million years ago; stumps at Gilboa, New York, belong to tree-fern-like plants at least 26 feet (8 m) tall. A Late Devonian fish from Arctic Canada already had a neck and a wrist, features of four-legged animals. Sea life crashed at the Frasnian–Famennian boundary. On the map: North America and northern Europe side by side, and Gondwana over the South Pole.

periods.name: Silurian
periods.text: Plants big enough to see appear in the fossil record by the Late Silurian, about 425 million years ago, some 50 million years after the first spores. Continents were colliding in what are now Newfoundland and the Maritime Appalachians. Smaller extinction crises in the Silurian seas are linked to warming and oxygen-poor water. On the map: Africa and South America, then part of Gondwana, lie at high southern latitudes; North America and northern Europe sit close together south of the equator.

periods.name: Ordovician
periods.text: Sea life multiplied: reefs built by animals, more complex sea-floor communities and much richer plankton. The first land plants left spores about 475 million years ago. The period ended in the Hirnantian with a short, intense glaciation at the South Pole and two pulses of extinction that removed about 85% of marine species, the first of the big five. On the map: Gondwana reaches from the tropics to the South Pole, painted white in the far south on the last two Ordovician maps.

periods.name: Cambrian
periods.text: The Cambrian begins where burrows of mobile animals appear in the rock. Exactly when is still being refined: Scotese’s atlas uses 542 million years ago, today’s chart 538.8 ± 0.6, and rocks in Namibia 538.6–538.8. Early in the Cambrian many animal groups appear as fossils, apparently within a few million years, though their lineages are tens of millions of years older. On the map: almost all land lies south of the equator, most of it in Gondwana.

periods.name: Ediacaran
periods.text: The first large, complex living things appear: the soft-bodied Ediacara biota, from about 575 million years ago. At Mistaken Point, Newfoundland, the oldest are 574.17 ± 0.66 million years old. Some were early animals; others may have been failed experiments. Later ones could move, and by 550 million years ago some had calcified parts. On the 600-million-year map: white at high latitudes, most of it in the south.

periods.name: Cryogenian
periods.text: Two long ice ages. The first, the Sturtian, lasted from about 717 to 660 million years ago, and its ice reached the sea near the equator. Whether the whole planet froze into a snowball Earth is a hypothesis, built on rocks such as Namibia’s, where glacial deposits are capped by carbonate laid down as the climate flipped to an extreme greenhouse. On the map: Scotese’s 690-million-year map, from the middle of the Sturtian, paints no ice.

measured.30: share of painted land within 30 degrees of the equator on map 93, cos-latitude weighted; 60_story.py re-measures it (claim tonian-land-tropics)

periods.name: Tonian
periods.text: The oldest map in the atlas, 750 million years ago. Rodinia, the supercontinent before Pangaea, later broke apart; its rifted edge, formed from the Neoproterozoic into the early Paleozoic, became the margin of eastern North America. The major animal groups had not yet appeared as fossils. On the map: most land lies within 30° of the equator. East–west positions are the least certain part of a map this old: rock magnetism records latitude, not longitude.

prologue.text: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old. A zircon crystal from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, 4.404 billion years old, is the oldest evidence of continental crust and oceans. Oxygen first built up in the air in the Great Oxidation Event, which began between 2.46 and 2.43 billion years ago. This atlas has no map older than 750 million years, so the story here is told in words.
prologue.title: Before 750 million years ago
